title: Opus: water pours, falls and levels like water - continuous falls, basins that fill level, nothing lost (b5de1ca, N61O)
author: Opus
note: Measured first, in stone on level ground (seed 7): a tank 300 cells up with its side knocked out, a walled basin under it, and a slope. The fall was a dotted line: each column of the lip let go one cell a tick and the cells fell 6 rows a tick, so 46 of every 60 rows of the fall held no water. The tank took 8 s to empty and never drained its last layer. The basin never levelled: its surface still sloped 13 cells after 20 s, because only single surface cells crept downhill where the surface stepped down by 2. Now, in pw-sim: (1) Water with a long way to fall goes as drops in flight, with the speed it left at: out of a breach at sqrt(2 g h), as a sliding sheet at its run, over a lip at a trickle. Gravity takes it from there. So a fall comes off its lip as an arc, whole at the top and thinning as it speeds up, and the drops go back into the water where they land. A sheet or lump with nothing under it falls whole. (2) A lake draining through a hole pours as fast as its depth drives it (the same rule as a breach in its side). (3) Water finds its level: a surface cell looks along the surface, through the water, up to 128 cells either way, for where it stands lowest or where it runs over an edge, and goes there. So a basin fills level from wherever the water comes in, and water left on a ledge runs off. Result on the same test: the tank empties in about 4 s, down to 1 cell (it was 8 s, with 190 left). The fall is a continuous sheet of drops. The basin levels to within 2 cells (a 0.5% slope, level to the eye) by 8 s, where before it still sloped 13 cells after 20 s. Water down the slope moves about twice as fast. A tunnel under a breached lake floods 73-76% in 5 s (it was 55%). The fall now takes as long as a real fall: it starts at rest at the lip and gravity speeds it up. Before, it moved at full speed from the first moment. Water is kept to the cell everywhere: drops in flight count as the world's water. A ground sag that pressed water out sideways into a hollow used to turn that water into rubble; now it goes as water (pw-stability). Cost: the water sim is no dearer (a lake breached by two large blasts: p95 3.2 ms, as before). Frames are unchanged in real time (median 13.3 ms, p95 13.5 ms), with up to 7,600 drops in flight. Suites 17/17 on seeds 7, 3 and 11, with new pw-physics checks (all fail on the old code): water pours out of a breach and falls as a sheet of drops, the tank empties, the basin levels, and the falling water is all kept.

title: Opus: falling pieces of buildings tip, slide and settle - no more spinning in the rubble (c3655bf, N49O)
author: Opus
note: Measured on your seed (370934178) with BLAST L on its tallest towers, before changing anything. The big pieces turned calmly (2 rad/s at most). The spinning was in the medium chunks of 36 to 300 cells: up to 40 rad/s (six turns a second) while touching the rubble, some turning nearly two full turns and still going 10 s after the blast. Four causes, each fixed in pw-fragments with physics rather than a cap: (1) Each contact was reduced to one point, so friction there kept turning a chunk over and it rolled along like a wheel. Now a piece lies on a face: the push spreads across the face that touches, and turns the piece only once the turning is more than the push can hold across that face. What lands flat stays flat and slides to a stop, what lands on a corner tips over it, and what has its weight past the edge tips over that edge. Loose rubble or earth gives under a piece and closes round it, so a piece that comes down in a heap stops turning. (2) Ploughing through rubble was free: the rubble was thrown aside but never pushed back. Now every cell of rubble a piece throws aside takes its momentum out of the piece at that point, so pieces slow and stop in a heap. (3) A piece that shattered on a hard blow passed the whole blow's turn to its chunks, as if it had pivoted on its corner. Now the blow goes into the breaking, and the chunks keep a quarter of that turn. (4) A blast's push set a piece's far edge moving as fast as the whole push. The wave meets a piece near its middle, so it now turns a building's piece by a quarter of that (trees still go end over end). Also: a piece shaken down to too little frame now comes apart as rubble instead of flying on empty, and a piece that sheds cells now turns about where its weight really is. Result in pw-collapse (seeds 7, 3, 11): the most any falling piece turns, all told, is 98 deg, 76 deg and 106 deg, where before it was 944 deg and 542 deg on seeds 7 and 3. No piece turns more than half a turn. On your seed, the only things that still tumble are small chunks about 1 m across thrown by the blast, at most about two-thirds of a turn while they fly. Ruins: pieces now come to rest in the heap on their own lot (24 to 35 ruins at once, where before about 9 got thrown clear), and the builders clear them as they rebuild. So the pw-collapse ruin check now counts the most ruins lying at once, not what is left after 30 s. Suites 17/17 on seeds 7, 3 and 11, with a new pw-collapse check that falling pieces never spin.

title: Opus: a deep flood brings a tower down - water pushes with its real pressure, and none of it is lost (ae40a09, N42O)
author: Opus
note: Your flood test, re-run first on the current branch: the column of water 140 cells (about 10 m) deep broke 167 of the tower's 13,398 wall cells and stopped, and the tower stood at full health with 95 cells of water still against it after 30 s. Two reasons. (1) A wall's breaking was judged by the water's speed, which grows only with the square root of the depth, so deep water was far too weak (the depth was also only read up to 128 cells, and walls inside flooded rooms were never pushed). (2) Nothing judged the water's push on the building as a whole: a tower stands on its back walls, which the water runs past, so no flood could ever bring one down. Now: (1) A wall gives way where the water's pressure is more than it holds. The pressure is the depth of water standing over it (traced up through a flooded room's ceiling to where the water stands open), plus v²/2g where the water runs at it, minus any water on its far side. What a wall holds goes with its material's hardness and its thickness squared, the way a wall panel bends between floors: a 20 cm brick wall holds about 1.25 m of water, and glass almost none. (2) Each storey must take the push of all the water against the building above it: the depth standing against its upstream side minus that against its downstream side. Water as deep on both sides pushes nothing, an open frame (a hall on pillars) only by the share its frame fills, and a side dug into the ground is held by the ground. Each frame cell across the storey takes a set amount by its hardness (back wall counted as brick: in this side view about a twentieth of the building's depth is brick facade, which shears at about 0.3 MPa). If a storey can't take the push, everything above it gives way and is shoved off downstream, as fast as the extra push over its weight gives it. Result on your test: the tower's ground storey takes 4,004 and the water pushed 7,198, so it tips over away from the water within a second and comes down in a heap. From each building's frame, the depth of still water against one side that would sweep it: the towers 70 to 95 cells (5 to 7 m), depending on how long they are; the open hall next to it about 60; the military bases about 130 (9 m). Checked on seed 7 with the same 140-cell flood: five towers of similar strength all come down; the same tower stands under 90 cells (6 m); the concrete military base stands under 140. Water: in the test, a core settling back into its flooded vault overwrote 41 water cells. WGM fixed that in pw-cores (2b013de). With it every water cell is kept, counted with the spray in the air, on all seeds. Cost: the water sim is unchanged (p95 0.3 ms when nothing falls). The structure check adds about 0.15 ms a tick while a flood is new; the first look at a big tower is about 9 ms. A swept tower costs no more than a blasted one. Suites 17/17 on seeds 7, 3 and 11. pw-physics now checks that 140 cells of water sweep the tallest tower, that 60 cells leave another standing, and that no water is lost.

title: Opus: falling trees never sink into the ground, their limbs bend where they strike, snapped branches fall on their own (666e8f4, N41O)
author: Opus
note: Checked trees for the same problems as buildings first, measuring 10 trees felled on three seeds. (1) Clipping: yes. Small branch pieces sliding down slopes sank steadily into the turf, up to 71% of a twig's wood buried 2+ cells deep and as deep as 5 cells. A plant piece was only pushed back as far as it had moved in that step; it never took the "lying in it, work it back out" path that buildings got in N40O. Now a plant piece that lies in the ground is put back out by how deep it lies. Its wood never goes more than a cell under the surface (deepest 2 cells, the turf's top layer, on all three seeds; before, 3 to 5). (2) Rigid image: yes. A falling tree was one stiff picture until it landed. Now its thin limbs (branches and twigs thinner than its trunk and stoutest boughs) bend where they strike the ground. Each one bends about its joint, where it grows from stouter wood, the way a branch held at its root bends under a load at its end: hardly at all near the joint, most at the tip. Stiffness follows its girth (the same spring as a standing tree's swinging limb), and it springs back when released. Bent as far as it goes, it bears the tree's weight like the rest of the wood, or snaps if the blow or the load is more than its wood takes. The cells really move, so the limb is drawn and collides where it is, pixel by pixel. Fast-flying trees also lose leaves from the edge of the crown to the air. (3) Separated branches: partly. A branch snapped off in flight used to be stamped into the world where it broke. Now it falls on as a piece of its own with its own collision. A tree left in separate bits after a snap comes apart: its biggest part goes on as it was (limbs still bent and springing), and each other part becomes its own piece. Also, a standing tree's limb swinging after a blow now stops against the ground or a wall instead of passing through it. Cost: the falling-piece step averages 0.25 ms a tick with 10 trees coming down (0.22 before). The worst tick is about 4 ms, when a branch snaps and the tree is remade in the same tick. Suites 17/17 on seeds 7, 3 and 11, with new checks in pw-physics (all three fail on the old code): falling trees never sink into the ground, each falling piece is one body of wood, and limbs bend where they strike while snapped branches fall as pieces of their own.

title: Your afternoon requests: hollow buildings fold like boxes, landslides gather speed, burnt forests (9382ccf, 78b9d90)
note:
- Break-up by what a piece hits: rock and concrete crack it sooner and throw its rubble fast and far, down the slope; soil and sand take the blow (dented, clods thrown); water slows it and splashes. A long piece landing across a ridge or a corner snaps over it.

A blast still only starts slides where it hits: the untouched world stands still.

The ground is charred, boulders sooted (they no longer burn away), and burnt trunks often smoulder for a minute or so.
- Shed leaves drift down to the ground instead of vanishing in mid-air.
- Your design notes are in the plan: F2 (buildings grow pillars-first from their cores) and C (mountain bunkers with firing openings and reinforced rock).

title: Step A2.11 done: falling buildings are one physics system now - they tip all the way over and break apart as they land (c5bbbd5)
note:
- What you saw: when a falling building landed, the whole piece was turned into loose debris at once, which rained down in the building's outline (the "ghost"). Tipping pieces were also being switched to a straight drop partway through the fall, so they stopped midway.
- Now every falling piece is one solid body with real contact physics. What it strikes pushes back at the point of contact, with friction, so it bounces, slides and turns over what it lands on.
- A tower losing one side leans as the storeys at its foot are crushed into the ground under it. It goes all the way over onto its side.
- Hard blows break off the corner that took them, thrown out the way the building was falling. A harder blow cracks it along jagged lines into chunks that carry on from exactly where they were, still drawn as the building, with no switch to a debris sprite. Each chunk keeps its own share of the motion and can crack again once.
- Chunks that come to rest stay as ruins: whole pieces of the building, tilted and out of place.
- A heavy piece flattens a weaker building it lands on (the greenhouse below).
- Air: a falling building drives the air with it, so its dust rolls out the way it fell. A floor coming straight down blows dust and grit out of both sides at its base.
- Dust: falling rubble used to erase the dust it landed in. Now it pushes the dust up out of its way, and collapse dust hangs longer.
- A damaged building is re-checked every second or so, so no bit of it is left floating when what propped it slides away.
- Also in this commit: trees topple whole when blasted, and only a very close, strong blast breaks them at the boughs and trunk; charred trees; walls count in a building's spans.
All 16 test suites pass on seeds 7, 3 and 11. Next: landslides (more of the mountain comes off, sooner), then foliage regrowing on wrecked ground.

title: Step A2.5 done: everything moves by the same rules from the element table (e4cc578)
note:
- The element table now holds how each material moves: how readily it slides off a slope, how far it spreads, what it packs down into, how fast a gas rises and thins. The cell simulation reads these instead of keeping its own lists.

title: Plan: step by step (reordered so each step builds on the last)
note:
Each step is tested on three seeds and committed to the work branch before the next one starts. Why this order:
- The terrain comes first, because everything after it is placed on it.
- Cores come before the pipeline (the pipe runs through the cores).
- Repair comes after cores (it runs through their translators).
- Seeds come after cores, pipeline and the steep rule.
- City growth comes after seeds, then the economy, farms and military that run on it.
The shadow tentacles are designed into each structure as it is built.

steps.text: A0.1 Soil: dark topsoil with roots and tongues into the subsoil; subsoil regions (brown earth / loess / red laterite)
A0.2 Roads built up in courses into the earth (asphalt -> crushed stone -> sand/gravel -> compacted subgrade)
A0.3 Pockets of flat land across the map; no pop/farm/core/mine buildings on too-steep ground
A0.4 Simpler Chinese dragons on stronger pedestals
A0.5 Smoke drifts in eddies and thins instead of hanging in one spot
A0.6 ROAD tool removed (roads come only from towns spreading)
A0.7 Mine conveyor HM (and pipe cargo) no longer drawn in front of crates and drums

A. Debris and gas: a collapsed piece rains down instead of standing as a column; debris spreads out flatter and faster; dense gas pours like rain; blasts throw building debris back in a plume and break back walls, ladders and fittings (tunnels too)

A2.1 Physics: one element table for every material, Powder Toy style (weight, state, gravity, drag, diffusion, hardness, cohesion, pressure strength, heat). Rock far tougher than dirt in blasts: blast strength is shielded by the hard material between a cell and the blast

A2.2 Avalanches: each ground material has cohesion (how far it can overhang); when a blast cuts away its support, the ground breaks loose and slides down the mountain as a landslide, cascading until stable

A2.3 Landslides that FLOW: released ground pours down the slope as a fast granular stream with dust over it; no slots, pillars or floating pieces left behind | trees break apart and fly or catch fire; everything left above a blast falls; towers dropping into their footprint break apart as they sink into their own rubble
A2.3b Repair around the new ground, even while it is still settling: pipes re-route in one smooth run around craters and slides; tunnels dig out the rubble and re-line; buildings in step F

A2.4 Air: a coarse pressure and wind grid (active only near blasts) that pushes smoke, dust and flying debris, blows out weak walls and glass, and kicks up loose ground | also: street lamps, gates and furniture topple when struck instead of leaving pieces hanging in the air

A2.5 Unified movement: every moving cell (debris, earth, water, gas) moves by the same rules from the element table: heavier sinks through lighter, fast things fly with velocity and settle back into the grid

A2.6 Pipes are part of the background wall: across tunnels, shafts and caves they run on the wall face, behind every timber, lamp, ladder, rail, crate and plant; they cross caves the same way instead of diving under them (and no more endless re-laying where they met a cave) | in developed tunnels too: the pipes are built into the finished wall design, not hidden behind it

A2.7 Trees break in parts, not all at once: a hit knocks off leaves, snaps a branch or breaks the trunk where it is struck (no chain reaction of whole trees exploding when their debris hits each other)
A2.8 Fire on trees: burnt trees stand as black, charred, leafless snags that are brittle and break into more dust; wood burns longer than leaves
A2.9 Blasts scorch buildings: the walls and floors around an impact are darkened

A2.10 Smoother landslides: a cut face taller than its ground can hold (soil about 1 m, rock 4-5 m) fails as a wedge that topples off and pours down the slope, again and again until the talus at its foot props it; no more straight seams where the check stopped

A2.11 Building collapses: the lower part sinking into its own rubble breaks up visibly, piece by piece, instead of vanishing into a smooth grey cone; a destroyed building keeps some of its structure as misplaced, unstable chunks; pieces that came away whole become ruins - part of the terrain - that city repair and growth later clear and recycle into HM | walls carry the building: a back wall alone does not hold a roof up, so a building whose walls are blasted away comes down

A2.12 Trees ride landslides: a tree whose ground slides away comes down with it as one piece and ends up lying on the slope, losing a few leaves, instead of bursting apart (blasts still tear trees up more)
A2.13 Foliage grows back on wrecked ground (grass, then bushes and saplings), slowly, from the plants still standing round it (e6e0d68, by the Game of Life)
A2.15 Falling buildings are hollow boxes: weight in the frame, rooms open, they fold where they land; rubble mostly from structure; break-up depends on what they hit (rock, soil, water, ridges)
A2.16 Landslides gather momentum (grains over steep edges run on as particles); slides keep going while their ground runs off; leaning cliffs fail
A2.17 Burnt forests: ash dusting, charred black snags and ground, sooted boulders, smouldering trunks

A2.18 Trees grown wood-first (trunk, branches, then leaves along the branches); no leaves without wood; trees fall over when their ground is hollowed out; core bunker block on pillars; nothing anywhere left floating (only arches of dense material span a gap)
A2.19 Leaves in front of the branches (the wood still there behind them, for breaking and burning)
A2.20 Debris holds as it lies - even a straight-up stack - until vibration or wind pushes it (heavier takes more); then it topples and spills (232c7f9)

A2.21 Sinkholes: ground over a void sinks slowly into a bowl sized by the hole, terrain, trees and buildings with it; the hole stopes upward until it breaches. No more vertical chimneys of dirt | a thin roof over a big blasted hole caves in, so the mountain top above it comes down (your screenshot) | slender columns and spires of rock or earth left standing free (taller than about 3 times their width for rock, 1.5 for soil) topple and come down, big ones as one piece | done: sags and chokes (524df60), slender rock columns topple (a3a2ede)
A2.22 Trees: the base decides whether one stands; cut loose, it falls free under wind, terrain, shape and weight, and its branches bend where they hit (stiffer the thicker) (1644686, 50ec25f)

A2.23 Blast smoke: a near-round cloud racing out from the fireball in every direction, a few tongues reaching further, braking hard (exponentially) to an ordinary drift; only the ground and walls near the blast shape it
A2.24 Nothing floats unless it is held at its sides: thin leftover strips of buildings, and back walls with nothing round them, come down (cb53f32)
A2.25 Shadows fade out softly (anisotropic: a long soft fade along the surface, a short one across it); no hard edges or blocky patches in the ground shading

A2.26 Pancake while tipping: the weight of a tipping top crushes the storeys it is tipping from, row by row across their whole width, and then its own lowest storeys, so it comes down storey by storey as it leans (a light top stalls on a stump that can hold it)

A2.27 Pillars always reach the bottom: the core bunker gets a pair of pillars beside its core on the pit floor; every pillar (bunker, slope stages: timber posts, gothic piers, modern pilotis) goes down column by column to the ground under it

A2.28 Blast smoke takes its shape from the space round it: the blast's smoke is driven into the open cells round it, nearest first along the ways open to it, so it funnels along tunnels, through rooms and out of doors and broken windows; thick where it is cramped, thin and patchy in the open; 18% faster
A2.29 Collapsing buildings spill out sideways, low and wide, top and bottom; smoke 35% thinner (9b7fba0)

A2.30 Things break into chunks as their stuff does: earth a powder with odd clods, rock and concrete jagged lumps with dust, a building's frame slabs, lengths and blocks with shrapnel, wood lengths of trunk and branch with splinters; back walls come away in panels (2e2ca02)
A2.31 Falling pieces no longer slide through the ground: where a piece drives into the ground or another building, its bottom breaks apart there (aa2dbec)
A2.32 Blasts throw back what they break loose - felled trees, boughs, pieces of building - as hard as the blast over the piece's weight (aa2dbec)

B. World 2.2x larger, closer to your nature refs: more rugged, real transitions between flats and mountains, pyramid-like mountains (broad base, straight flanks), rocks dense at summits and bases; flat pockets kept | done (ee9cb07): grey jointed massif rock summit to foot, scree as the same rock broken small, laterite/loess belts fading off the flanks
